title: Childhood tin flute and kids behind the second line
summary: He taught himself the tin flute as a boy, and kids with flutes and tin pans followed parades, trying to play along with the band.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: I was going to ask some more about, to go way back to your childhood again. This little tin flute you played, where did you play that? Did you learn that just watching anybody or learning the street or where did you play it?

I just picked it up myself. I mean, at that time the kids was, they was buying them but just blowing them, you know? Yeah. But I went on and got me one and I used to play songs on it. I could play it real good. And people used to like to, you have me play it like on Saturday evening, man, I'd get on the grocery car and blow that thing and I didn't know what kiddie was but people would get a big kick out of it, you know? Like a bunch of white people might pass in the court and see me blowing and stopping. First thing you know, they draw big congregation around. Every crowd of the Yemi play the flute. Yeah, I often talk about that. I say, some instruments are mad and it's gifted to a poet. I mean, I could take one of them things and play any song on it that I would get.
Somebody told me once some of the kids used to play them on the parades, like the second line kids. I never did see any of that. Did they ever do that?

Oh, no. Yeah, well we all used to play behind the second line. You see, the second line wasn't like the yesterday. I mean, it's run away with it now. You can't get to see a club for a second line. In the olden times it was different. You see now they would have the tally holes. You remember the tally holes? Well, they used to have the tally holes. And most likely the women would be in the tally holes. They'd have the tally holes all decorated with paper ribbon and things. And the men would walk in front and the tally holes behind. The second liners would stay on the bank and they didn't just have to have five or six policemen to try to keep it. You could get a viewing of the parade, what it looked like, you know. And we kids would be on the bank with them floots, like you said, blowing them. But we couldn't go like the kids go now. We maybe could go three or four blocks and we'd turn around and go back home. But our parents didn't allow us further than that, you know. What did you do?
Try to play the same piece right along with the band?

Yeah, you'd be trying to play what they would be playing. And we'd go three or four blocks and then get in another section and pick up maybe a gang of floots. Or maybe a gang of flute players or tin pan players there. They'd beat on boxes and things. Go ahead and have their portion on the sidewalk. You know, file in the parade and they'd go their distance and they had to come back. Because there was more restriction on the kids then than there is now. You see, that old fire in John House up there on Maple Street. And that bell used to ring every night at nine o'clock. Sometime I'd be four and five blocks off from my house when it first hit. But by the time it finished it, I'd be home and sometimes I'd be so scared I'd jump in the bed with my feet full of mud. Be scared to stop the washing. That's just how strict the older people was then. But now the majority of the people, they don't even know where they children is.
